newsitem.title: MEXICO: Dying woman brings rebel struggle to Mexico City.
newsitem.headline: Dying woman brings rebel struggle to Mexico City.

text.p: A dying Indian woman who has become a symbol of armed struggle in the jungle of southern Mexico arrived triumphantly in the capital on Friday in a publicity coup for the Zapatista rebels.

Commander Ramona stepped off a government plane wearing traditional Tzotzil Indian dress and was met by hundreds of cheering supporters overjoyed at seeing their first Zapatista guerrilla leader in the Mexican capital.
Stricken by cancer, she had asked to be allowed to attend an Indian rights congress in Mexico City as her dying wish.
The government, seeking to avoid the collapse of peace talks, agreed to allow the terminally ill leader to travel to the capital on her first-ever flight in an airplane.

The Zapatistas launched an armed rebellion in January 1994 in which more than 140 people died, but have so far confined their actions to their native state of Chiapas on Mexico's southern border with Guatemala.
Ramona arrived aboard an Interior Ministry plane, flanked by Mexican congressmen, after days of tortuous negotiations with the government of President Ernesto Zedillo.

But for the festive reception crowd, which blasted horns, waved flags and chanted the initials of the Zapatista National Liberation Army, it was as if the rebels had won their way to Mexico City by force of arms.

"It's very important that they finally broke the (military) cordon. The Zapatistas can come out," gushed Elisa Benavides, a leader of the Zapatistas' political wing who was coordinating the party-like reception in a private hanger owned by Mexican airline Taesa.
Ramona, her face hidden by a trademark Zapatista black ski-mask, touched a chord among many Mexicans with her unexpected odyssey from a dirt-poor village in Chiapas state to Mexico City.

Her trip was a clever publicity stunt at a time when the rebels, who rose up for Indian rights and democratic reform, have broken off peace talks with the government and were slipping from the media spotlight.

The government, which has long been anxious to keep the rebel struggle bottled up in Chiapas, had threatened at first to arrest Zapatista leaders if they attended the four-day National Indian Congress.
But it backed down, apparently because the infirm Ramona -- one of the guerrillas' most respected leaders before she was struck down with cancer two years ago -- was a suitable compromise figure.
The Zapatistas' charismatic leader Subcommander Marcos, who was to be the star of the event, stayed behind in the Chiapas jungle.

Both sides sought to profit from the visit, the Zapatistas on the grounds that it took their struggle to Mexico City at last, and the government because it showed it was capable of offering an olive branch.
